claim: There is a 50-fold increase in body weight during murine postnatal development, 50% of which is contributed by skeletal muscle.
source: There is a 50-fold increase in body weight during murine postnatal development, 50% of which is contributed by skeletal muscle (Allen et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Allen et al., 1979.

claim: Myofiber number remains constant after birth in rodents.
source: After a period of active proliferation of myogenic progenitor satellite cells and fusion to form myofibers during late embryonic development, myofiber number remains constant after birth.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Satellite cells make up approximately 11% of muscle nuclei at postnatal day 14.
source: Satellite cells make up approximately 11% of muscle nuclei at postnatal day 14, but by week 17, the fraction of satellite cell nuclei drops to 3% (Ontell et al., 1984)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ontell et al., 1984.

claim: By week 17, the fraction of satellite cell nuclei drops to 3%.
source: Satellite cells make up approximately 11% of muscle nuclei at postnatal day 14, but by week 17, the fraction of satellite cell nuclei drops to 3% (Ontell et al., 1984)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ontell et al., 1984.

claim: The tibialis anterior muscle cross-sectional area increases seven-fold from postnatal day 1 (PN1) to PN28 in mice.
source: The tibialis anterior muscle cross-sectional area increases seven-fold from postnatal day 1 (PN1) to PN28 in mice with a concomitant five-fold increase in maximal isotonic force (Gokhin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gokhin et al., 2008.

claim: There is a concomitant five-fold increase in maximal isotonic force from PN1 to PN28 in mouse tibialis anterior muscle.
source: The tibialis anterior muscle cross-sectional area increases seven-fold from postnatal day 1 (PN1) to PN28 in mice with a concomitant five-fold increase in maximal isotonic force (Gokhin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gokhin et al., 2008.

claim: There is a six-fold increase in intrinsic mechanical function from PN1 to PN28 that is size-independent.
source: Importantly, while the increased isotonic force is due primarily to increased muscle size, there is a six-fold increase in intrinsic mechanical function from PN1 to PN28 that is size-independent.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the context of postnatal muscle development.

claim: T-tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum rapidly mature within the first 3 weeks after birth.
source: T-tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum, the cellular structures required for excitation contraction coupling, rapidly mature within the first 3 weeks after birth (Franzini-Armstrong, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Franzini-Armstrong, 1991.

claim: The majority of skeletal muscles in mice switch from slow, type I fibers to fast, type II fibers.
source: The majority of skeletal muscles in mice switch from slow, type I fibers to fast, type II fibers (Agbulut et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Agbulut et al., 2003.

claim: Fast fibers have different cytosolic calcium concentrations of 30 nM.
source: In addition to the differences in metabolism, fast and slow fibers have different cytosolic calcium concentrations of 30 nM and 50–60 nM, respectively (Gailly et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gailly et al., 1993.

claim: Slow fibers have cytosolic calcium concentrations of 50–60 nM.
source: In addition to the differences in metabolism, fast and slow fibers have different cytosolic calcium concentrations of 30 nM and 50–60 nM, respectively (Gailly et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gailly et al., 1993.

claim: Ninety-five percent of human intron-containing genes are alternatively spliced.
source: Ninety-five percent of human intron-containing genes are alternatively spliced; however, opinions differ with regard to the extent to which this huge diversity is regulated to provide a functional outcome (Tress et al., 2017; Pickrell et al., 2010; Gonzàlez-Porta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tress et al., 2017; Pickrell et al., 2010; Gonzàlez-Porta et al., 2013.

claim: The majority of alternative splicing is not conserved.
source: Several studies have shown that the majority of alternative splicing is not conserved; however, alternative exons that are tissue-specific or regulated during periods of physiological change show high levels of conservation of the variable protein segment, suggesting functional importance
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from several studies.

claim: Alternative exons that are tissue-specific or regulated during periods of physiological change show high levels of conservation of the variable protein segment.

claim: All four calcineurin A exons underwent a nearly complete switch to the fetal pattern following ASO delivery.

claim: Non-targeting ASOs had no effect on calcineurin A splicing.

claim: The fetal isoforms of at least Ppp3ca and Ppp3cb have intrinsically higher phosphatase activity than the adult isoforms.
source: Since these genes are up-regulated in response to redirected calcineurin splicing in FDB muscle and down-regulated upon loss of NFATC3 activity in C2C12 cultures, these results strongly suggest that the fetal isoforms of at least Ppp3ca and Ppp3cb have intrinsically higher phosphatase activity than the adult isoforms

claim: Alternative splicing transitions during postnatal skeletal muscle development impact muscle physiology.

claim: Redirected splicing of calcineurin A to the fetal isoforms promotes nuclear localization of calcineurin target Nfatc3.
